title: Israel election results live: count of absentee ballots under way as coalition talks set to begin
text:
From 3h agoIsrael’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalitionEmma Graham-HarrisonHours before the final results from Israel’s elections were in, several things were clear. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition had lost its mandate, and the opposition had a firm majority.But most of Israel’s Jewish opposition ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties, in the course of a racist election campaign in which Netanyahu painted Palestinian citizens as an enemy inside the state.The self-imposed ban on a broader opposition alliance, if it holds, offers Netanyahu the prospect of turning his defeat into another term in office – or at least a prolonged mandate as caretaker prime minister and perhaps another round of elections.This confected barrier to unseating Netanyahu became the focus of Israeli media and analysts. “No Clear Government” announced the newspaper Israel Hayom. “Road to Unity Government Has Been Paved”, read an article on Channel 12.Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, holds his daughter as he casts his vote in Maghar, Israel. Photograph: Rami Shlush/ReutersYair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, attacked that framing. “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count,” he said in a statement calling for a government with Palestinians, who make up about 20% of Israel’s population.“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.”While Palestinian-led parties do not describe themselves as Zionist, neither do some of the ultra-Orthodox groups who are a key part of Netanyahu’s current coalition.A survey taken as polls closed on election day showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with the Palestinian-led Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu, political psychology researcher Eran Halperin said.But opposition leaders were silent on Wednesday, as they apparently tried to balance their desire to unseat Netanyahu with promises against working with Palestinians.Former general Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the biggest opposition party, has not directly ruled out governing with Palestinians but laid out conditions that made it politically impossible for them to join a coalition.Palestinians have been clearer about their priorities. “We are ready and prepared to pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government,” Yousef Jabareen, leader of the larger Joint List, said on Wednesday. “The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership.”Key events8m agoBen-Gvir calls for arrest of Arab political leaders55m agoIsrael police dismiss claims election 'stolen' by Arab parties - report3h agoIsrael’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition4h agoFinal ballots being tallied with results expected to show no clear winnerBen-Gvir calls for arrest of Arab political leadersIsrael’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has called for the arrest of leaders of Arab political parties, citing unsubstantiated claims of foreign funding.In a post on X, he said the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security service, “must order, as early as this morning, the arrest of the leaders of the Arab parties suspected of involvement with Qatari funds”, without clarifying further.The Shin Bet has not responded to the allegations.As reported earlier, Israeli police and the central elections committee have said there is no evidence of election fraud.Israel police dismiss claims election 'stolen' by Arab parties - reportIsraeli police have dismissed claims by Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party that the election was “stolen” by parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, according to comments reported by Hebrew-language media outlets.A police source, as quoted by the Times of Israel, said:
 double quotation markElection day passed with very few irregular incidents concerning the integrity of the election, even when compared to previous elections.
 It should be emphasised that there is no investigative- or intelligence-based supporting evidence for the claims.
Dean Livne, the acting director general of Israel’s central elections committee, said there was “no basis for allegations of election theft”, the Israeli Kan radio reported. The committee said yesterday that it had received a complaint by the Likud party alleging Arab parties had compromised election integrity, which it would review as part of its routine post-election process.As vote counting continues, parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel are projected to win 19 seats after Tuesday’s election, driven by record-high turnout among the Arab population.Israeli news website Ynet is reporting that just over 29,000 of the absentee ballots have been counted so far, out of an estimated 500,000.According to Ynet, Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is leading among these ballots, with 18.5% of the votes of far. The Together alliance of Naftali Bennet and Yair Lapid comes in second with 15.6%, while Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar is third, with 14.8%.The absentee ballots are afforded to people unable to return to their registered polling stations on election day. They include many in the IDF, as well as diplomats, prisoners and people in hospital.Experts say that the final tally of the absentee ballots is unlikely to significantly shift the current seat projection.Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Joint List – which represents a number of Israeli Arab parties – has told the ⁠Reuters news agency his party will seek to use its projected 11 seats “to facilitate getting rid of Netanyahu’s government and hopefully help to change the political situation in Israel.”Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc is currently projected to receive 48 seats, well short of the 61 needed to form a majority government, but many in his bloc have ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties which are projected to win 19 seats in total.Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, and a junior partner in Eisenkot’s bloc, has backed the idea of working with the parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel. But he is so far the only opposition leader making that call.Head of the Joint List alliance Yousef Jabareen speak on election night. Photograph: Jamal Awad/EPAJabareen said the Joint ​List could not join an Eisenkot-led government because of its support for Israel’s ‌military campaign in Gaza and occupation of southern Lebanon. But ‌he has left open the possibility of bolstering Eisenkot’s bloc from the outside, propping up a minority government through confidence votes.
 double quotation markWe have our demands to protect our community, to ‌advance the rights of our community and to promote equality for our community.”
The other main Palestinian party, Ra’am, is led by Mansour Abbas, who joined Naftali Bennett’s government in 2021, the first time an independent Arab party had entered an Israeli coalition. That government collapsed after 18 months, partly because of disagreements over the occupied West Bank.Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, casts his ballot alongside his family on Tuesday. Photograph: Mahmoud Illean/APAbbas has said he would ‌join an Eisenkot-led government. Speaking to Israeli media after voting wrapped on Tuesday night, Abbas said
 double quotation markI believe we can overcome the difficulties … and I think that most voters for the [Eisenkot] bloc do want to see a government with the Ra’am party.”
Throughout the elections campaign, Israel’s far-right demonized Palestinian citizens of Israel and branded Palestinian political participation as a threat to ​the state.Eisenkot himself ruled out forming a government with Palestinian parties during the campaign, citing what he called a lack of shared values, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state. However Abbas has claimed that senior members of Eisenkot’s bloc discussed ​a possible deal with him even before the election.Ameer Fakhoury, a political sociologist at Jerusalem’s Van Leer Institute, said that Palestinian votes may block Netanyahu and make an alternative government possible.
 double quotation markThe Jewish opposition may need Palestinian ⁠votes while refusing Palestinian partners. That is the central paradox.”
Israel’s ⁠currency, stocks and bonds came under ⁠pressure on Wednesday after initial election ​results showed prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc performing better-than-expected but falling short of a parliamentary majority.With 91% of votes tallied, Israeli media project Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc could win 53 seats, ahead ⁠of the 48 forecast for rival Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc but short of the 61 needed for a majority.Final results are expected on Thursday.An employee of the Israel central elections committee stands near a large screen that shows live results at the counting headquarters in the Knesset. Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAOn Wednesday the shekel weakened more ⁠than 2%, on course for its worst day since the aftermath of the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks and erasing Tuesday’s ​gains, when high voter turnout had raised expectations of a change in government.Tel ‌Aviv’s key benchmark stock index was ‌down 2.5%, its worst performance in more than four months.Opinion polls ahead of the election showing Eisenkot in ‌the lead had helped gains, with some investors expecting a change in government to improve relations with western allies.“Israel’s financial markets have reacted negatively to the result,” said William Jackson, chief emerging ‌markets economist at Capital Economics. He said the initial results offered Netanyahu more paths to remain in power, though any government that emerged was unlikely to be robust.
 double quotation markThe next government will probably be fragile.”
If neither Netanyahu nor ​Eisenkot can form a government, Israel could be facing another election, with Netanyahu remaining at the helm of a caretaker government in the meantime.Israel’s left-leaning newspaper Haaretz has published an editorial calling on the country’s opposition bloc to form a government with the Palestinian parties.With the combined number of Knesset seats for Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc and the grouping of Palestinian parties projected to be 67, the paper writes that Netanyahu’s government has “lost substantial support since the last round of elections.”
 double quotation markThe figures clearly point to an unprecedented achievement by the Arab community, which voted en masse for political partnership with Jews. Despite the challenges and reservations about voting, and amidst a particularly racist incitement campaign, a record 19 Knesset seats loudly and clearly declare: We are an inseparable part of this country.”
The editorial goes on to say that there is reason to believe that the leaders of Eisenkot’s change bloc will discard these “19 Knesset seats simply because they belong to Arab voters.”
 double quotation markThis would be a slap in the face to the citizens who went to the polls in droves to vote for integration.”
